notes: The congregation began in 1843 and erected this building; H. Rothget and John E. Strobbach enlarged it in 1847. It remained with the United Evangelical group after the 1848 split and was replaced by a brick church in 1854-55. Andreas printed pp. 350-351.

address_historical: north of present North Avenue near the lake
address_modern: near North Avenue and Lake Michigan
notes: Andreas says a small one-story building was erected in 1843 and burned early in 1845. Printed p. 597.

address_historical: southwest corner Wabash Avenue and Madison Street
structural_system: brick on stone foundation with Ionic portico
notes: Opened for services December 25, 1843 and consecrated in 1845; 55 by 112 feet including portico and cost about $4,000. Andreas printed pp. 291-292 and 505.

address_historical: west side LaSalle Street between Randolph and Washington streets
notes: Built and dedicated October 13, 1843, after an eight-week campaign; 40 by 72 feet and cost about $2,200. Destroyed by fire June 26, 1851. Andreas printed pp. 319-321.

canonical_name: Allan Robbins brick store near Lake and South Water
address_historical: near the Denker and Borges building at Lake and South Water streets
notes: A contemporary building-season description identifies a four-story 20-by-100-foot store but gives limited construction detail. Destruction in 1871 is inferred from location. Chicagology section Chicago Improvements 1844.

canonical_name: City Hotel to Sherman House enlargement
address_historical: City Hotel site; historical address requires parcel reconciliation
notes: The older City Hotel was remodeled in 1844 by adding two stories and renamed the Sherman House. This record represents the alteration, not original construction. Successive Sherman House rebuildings make demolition and fire fate ambiguous without parcel-level lifecycle work. Andreas hotel chapter printed pp. 633-636.

address_historical: junction of Lake Street and South Water Street
architect_or_builder: J. M. Van Osdel (architect); Robert Malcom (mason); Alexander Lloyd (builder)
structural_system: brick triangular building with circular corners and cast-iron balcony
notes: The building fronted 54 feet on Lake and 72 feet on South Water and cost about $5,500. Destruction in 1871 is inferred from location. Chicagology section Chicago Improvements 1844.

address_historical: southeast corner Washington and LaSalle streets
structural_system: brick with eight-foot basement, six-column Ionic portico, and 112-foot spire
notes: Church history dates erection to 1844; Andreas' architecture summary groups it with 1844-45 construction. It measured 55 by 80 feet, cost about $4,500, and burned October 20, 1852. Printed pp. 316-317 and 505-506.

address_historical: Washington Street near Clark Street Methodist Church
structural_system: frame on six-foot stone foundation; Ionic detailing
notes: Dedicated October 23, 1844; 30 by 45 feet and cost about $3,000. Later sold to Olivet Presbyterian after 1857; physical fate unresolved. Andreas printed p. 343 and p. 505.

address_historical: State Street between Lake and Randolph streets
architect_or_builder: J. M. Van Osdel (architect); Peter Page (mason); Campbell & Butler (builders)
structural_system: five brick buildings with Milwaukee pressed-brick fronts; each 20 by 50 feet
notes: Cost about $8,000. Kept as an aggregate record because the five component buildings are not separately named. Destruction in 1871 is inferred from location. Chicagology section Chicago Improvements 1844.

address_historical: South Water Street between Clark and Dearborn streets
architect_or_builder: J. M. Van Osdel (architect and superintendent); A. H. Heald (mason); P. L. Updike & Co. and Shepard & Johnson (builders)
owner_or_developer: P. E. W. Peck; Allan Robbins; John High Jr.; H. H. Magie
structural_system: four brick stores described as fireproof; each 20 by 120 feet
notes: The source treats this as four separately owned stores in one coordinated block; retained as one aggregate record until parcel identities are resolved. Cost $13,000. Destruction in 1871 is inferred from location. Chicagology section Chicago Improvements 1844.

address_historical: southwest corner Dearborn and Indiana streets
structural_system: brick with stone facings and central circular dome
notes: Cost about $3,500; first lecture December 11 and formal opening December 13, 1844. Andreas describes large lecture rooms, museum, library, and a Pantheon-like central feature. Printed pp. 464-466 and 505-506; Norris 1846 pp. 29 and 32 corroborates the college.

address_historical: Madison Street between Clark and LaSalle streets
notes: Cornerstone laid June 5, 1844; first service held August 25 after completion that month. Great Fire fate is inferred from the Loop location but later congregation/building history needs resolution. Andreas printed pp. 336-337.

address_historical: South Branch near North Street
owner_or_developer: Thomas Dyer; John P. Chapin; Julius Wadsworth
notes: Built in 1844 after Dyer and Chapin began packing in Reynolds' house; Julius Wadsworth joined them. The later Wadsworth & Dyer firm packed beef for the English market. Andreas printed pp. 562-563.

address_historical: Madison Street opposite the later McVicker's Theatre
architect_or_builder: Ira Miltimore (principal advocate and building agent; architectural attribution not established)
notes: Proposals were authorized in June 1844 and the first permanent public school was completed in spring 1845 for about $7,523.42. Norris calls it one of two large two-story brick schools. Andreas printed pp. 210-211; Norris 1846 pp. 6-7 and 26.

canonical_name: First Methodist Episcopal Church at Clark and Washington
address_historical: corner Clark and Washington streets
architect_or_builder: Sullivan and John M. Van Osdel (design features)
structural_system: brick with eight-foot stone basement and 148-foot spire
notes: Cornerstone laid May 8, 1845 and dedicated in November; 66 by 95 feet, capacity about 1,000, cost $12,000. Andreas printed pp. 325-327 and 505.

address_historical: north of present North Avenue near the lake
address_modern: near North Avenue and Lake Michigan
notes: Erected on the same site after the 1843 hospital burned early in 1845. Later fate is not stated in the cited passage. Andreas printed p. 597.

canonical_name: North Division School at Ohio and LaSalle
address_historical: corner Ohio and LaSalle streets
notes: Andreas says the 45-by-70-foot, two-story school arose in the 1844-45 program and was ready by 1846, costing about $4,000. Norris corroborates two large two-story brick schools completed within the preceding two years. Exact completion year and fate need review. Andreas printed pp. 210-211; Norris 1846 pp. 6-7 and 26.

canonical_name: St. Joseph's German Catholic Church first building
address_historical: northeast corner Chicago Avenue and Cass Street
structural_system: frame; 36 by 65 feet with small steeple
notes: Built in 1846 for about $900 and seating about 600. Later replaced after 1861; exact removal date and 1871 status need review. Andreas printed pp. 295-296.

canonical_name: St. Patrick's Catholic Church first building
address_historical: Desplaines Street between Randolph and Washington streets
notes: Opened April 12, 1846 and cost $750; later enlarged, moved to Desplaines and Adams, and used as a school. The cited source does not give the move date or final demolition. Andreas printed pp. 294-295.

canonical_name: St. Peter's German Catholic Church first building
address_historical: Washington Street between Wells and Franklin streets
owner_or_developer: St. Peter's German Catholic congregation under Rev. John Jung
structural_system: frame; 40 by 60 feet with small steeple
notes: Built in spring 1846 for about $900, seating about 700; moved with associated buildings in 1853 to Clark and Polk. Andreas printed pp. 294-295.

canonical_name: St. Peter's German Catholic rectory first building
address_historical: Washington Street between Wells and Franklin streets
notes: A separate frame rectory stood on the 1846 St. Peter's lot and was moved with the church property in 1853. Exact completion wording is less explicit than for the church. Andreas printed pp. 294-295.

canonical_name: St. Peter's German Catholic schoolhouse first building
address_historical: Washington Street between Wells and Franklin streets
notes: A separate frame schoolhouse stood on the 1846 St. Peter's lot and was moved with the church property in 1853. Exact completion wording is less explicit than for the church. Andreas printed pp. 294-295.

canonical_name: University of St. Mary of the Lake first campus building
address_historical: northeast quarter of block bounded by Chicago, Rush, Superior, and State streets
notes: Detailed chronology says foundations began October 17, 1845, the building was under roof November 22, and it opened July 4, apparently 1846, at a cost of $12,000. Another Andreas passage says completion in June 1845, creating an internal conflict. Fire fate is strongly indicated but should be checked against diocesan records. Andreas printed pp. 293 and 466-467; Norris 1846 pp. 29-32 corroborates the institution.

canonical_name: Dr. Edward Mead private insane asylum
address_historical: two miles north of the city; after temporary Kinzie Street quarters
notes: Andreas says Mead first used quarters on Kinzie Street, then purchased land two miles north and had a new asylum ready in 1847. Exact parcel, form, and later fate require review. Printed p. 597.

address_historical: south side Randolph Street, one or two lots east of southeast corner Dearborn Street
notes: A 40-by-80-foot frame completed in six weeks and opened June 28, 1847; totally destroyed by fire July 30, 1850. Andreas printed pp. 484-490.

address_historical: West Madison Street near Halsted Street
notes: Completed in May 1847 at a cost of $6,795. Its west-side location was outside the main 1871 burned district, but later demolition history remains unresolved. Andreas printed p. 212.

address_historical: vicinity of Madison Street and Ashland Avenue
notes: Opened in 1848 as an early makeshift cattle yard. It is included as a built complex rather than a single enclosed building; later closure date needs review. Andreas printed p. 564.

address_historical: possibly North Franklin Street at the river
owner_or_developer: R. C. Bristol or George Steel (sources conflict)
notes: Andreas' general manufacturing narrative credits R. C. Bristol with an elevator erected in 1848, while a biographical passage credits George Steel with the first steam elevator at North Franklin and the river, 100,000-bushel capacity, burned about 1854. This unresolved internal contradiction must not be silently normalized. Andreas printed pp. 580-581 and George Steel biographical passage.

canonical_name: First Norwegian Evangelical Lutheran Church building
address_historical: Superior Street between Wells and LaSalle streets
notes: After organizing February 14, 1848, the congregation bought an unfinished church that had blown down and rebuilt it for about $1,000; purchase cost $800. Sold in 1856. Andreas printed pp. 349-350.

canonical_name: Galena and Chicago Union Railroad first depot
address_historical: Kinzie Street and Canal Street
notes: The railroad's initial Chicago depot was at Kinzie and Canal. The 1849 Rees & Rucker map page explicitly describes the line running west from this depot; exact building completion and replacement history need confirmation from railroad records. Andreas' railroad chapter provides the 1848 opening context.

address_historical: north side near mouth of harbor
notes: McCormick arranged Chicago manufacture in 1847 and enlarged the manufactory near the harbor in 1848; this is an expansion record, not a claim that every component was newly built. Andreas printed p. 569.

address_historical: Market Street
notes: The Market Street works were established in 1848 and burned in 1854. The cited text does not explicitly state whether a new building was erected at establishment. Andreas printed p. 569.

address_historical: corner Canal and Adams streets
notes: The establishment began in 1848 and later built railroad cars and an early western locomotive. The source documents establishment, not unequivocal new construction, so the completion year is approximate. Andreas printed p. 568.

canonical_name: State Street Market Building and City Hall
address_historical: center of State Street, fronting Randolph Street and extending north toward Lake Street
original_use: market stalls municipal offices library and council chamber
architect_or_builder: John M. Van Osdel (architect and superintendent)
structural_system: two-story brick and stone building; 40 by 180 feet
notes: Erected beginning in January 1848 for $11,070; contained 32 ground-floor market stalls and city rooms above. Council first met there November 13, 1848. Andreas printed pp. 180-181.

address_historical: southeast corner State and Lake streets
notes: A later directory retrospective says Burton built the City Hotel in 1848 to Van Osdel's design. Destruction in 1871 is inferred from its Loop location and should be confirmed in a primary fire-loss list. Chicagology pre-fire transcription.

canonical_name: Charles Cleaver soap and candle factory on North Branch
address_historical: North Branch near Division Street
notes: Cleaver moved the factory here in 1849 and to Cleaverville in 1851. The source does not establish whether the North Branch premises were newly constructed. Andreas printed pp. 564-565.

address_historical: Eighteenth Street near the river
notes: Opened in May 1849 during the cholera emergency. Andreas does not give a demolition date; temporary status is explicit in context. Printed pp. 597-598.

address_historical: Erie Street between Wells Street and the river
architect_or_builder: Dr. Daniel Brainard or Dr. Levi Boone plan attribution requires review
notes: A second emergency hospital site described in the 1849 cholera narrative; neighbors threatened demolition. The OCR/source context associates its plan with Dr. Boone, but exact attribution and survival require page-image checking. Andreas printed pp. 597-598.

canonical_name: Holy Name Catholic Church first building
address_historical: southwest corner of St. Mary college grounds at Rush and Superior streets
architect_or_builder: Rev. Jeremiah Kinsella (project leader); Clowry and Breen (building committee)
notes: Begun in 1848, completed in 1849, and first used November 18, 1849. It was superseded as the parish/cathedral complex developed; exact removal date needs verification. Andreas printed pp. 296-297.

address_historical: Block 113, School District No. 2
notes: A brick school was ordered February 12, 1849 and completed December 17 for $9,745; it opened January 1850. Exact street address and individually documented fire fate need review; probable destruction is a spatial inference. Andreas printed pp. 213-214.

address_historical: Clark Street between Quincy and Adams streets
notes: Erected in 1849 on leased ground and identified by Andreas as Chicago's first synagogue; the congregation moved to a second building after the lease period. Andreas printed pp. 347-348.

canonical_name: St. Paul's German Evangelical Lutheran Church first building
address_historical: Indiana Street between Wells and Franklin streets
owner_or_developer: St. Paul's German Evangelical Lutheran congregation
notes: Built after the 1848 congregation split and ready in June 1849; replaced in the 1860s. Andreas printed pp. 349-350.

canonical_name: Chicago Gas Light and Coke Works
address_historical: South side of Monroe Street near Market Street
owner_or_developer: Chicago Gas Light and Coke Company
notes: Works and street mains began October 1849; plant completed August 1850 and Chicago's first public gas was supplied September 4, 1850. This is an industrial complex record, not a single building.

address_historical: Northwest corner Randolph and Dearborn Streets
architect_or_builder: John M. Van Osdel (architect, corroborating source); Robert Malcolm (mason); Shepherd & Johnson (builders)
notes: Opened in 1851; 80 feet on Randolph by 90 feet on Dearborn; reported cost $20,000. Raised about eight feet in 1859, an alteration that should be modeled separately.

address_historical: Northwest corner Lake and Dearborn Streets
architect_or_builder: John M. Van Osdel (architect and superintendent); C. and W. Price (masons); Updike & Sollitt (builders)
notes: Opened September 29, 1850; contemporary account gave a $75,000 building cost. Remodeled and enlarged in 1861, so late pre-fire views may not show the 1850 form unchanged.

address_historical: Block 87 of the school section; corner Polk and Wells Streets
structural_system: three-inch oak planks set upright; plank roof
notes: Opened December 1851. Main building measured about 100 by 24 feet and contained roughly 200 cells; David Walsh was first keeper.

canonical_name: Hamilton House at Clark and North Water
address_historical: Southeast corner Clark and North Water Streets
notes: Not new construction: the 1840 Washington House was moved from South Water near Clark in 1851, enlarged, remodeled, and renamed. Included as a major physical relocation/alteration; torn down spring 1868.

address_historical: Dearborn Street between Randolph and Washington Streets
architect_or_builder: John M. Van Osdel (architect); C. and W. Price (masons); Updike & Sollitt (builders)
notes: Completed January 1851 and opened in February. Building measured about 80 by 100 feet and had galvanized-iron cornices. The OCR of the reported cost is ambiguous, so cost is not normalized here.

address_historical: Washington Street at Wabash Avenue
notes: Cornerstone laid in 1849 and dedicated January 24, 1851. Approximately 73 by 130 feet, walls about 50 feet high, galleries, seating about 1,800, and stained glass.

address_historical: corner Washington Street and Wabash Avenue
notes: Included in the 1840s cohort because its cornerstone was laid in 1849; it was dedicated January 24, 1851. Andreas says it was destroyed in the 1871 fire. Printed pp. 304 and 505-506.

canonical_name: State Street Methodist Episcopal Church building
address_historical: Northwest corner State and Harrison Streets
notes: Not new construction: part of the former Second Presbyterian frame building was purchased, moved, and fitted for worship in spring/summer 1851. Retained because relocation materially changed Chicago's building inventory.

address_historical: Michigan Avenue near old Fort Dearborn
notes: Built 1850-51 at a reported cost of $50,000. This purpose-built federal hospital should not be confused with later Marine Hospital facilities.

address_historical: West Randolph Street near Canal Street
notes: Andreas identifies this as Chicago's first German theater and says it burned early in 1853. No dimensions or builder were found in the cited passage.

address_historical: Lake shore south of Twelfth Street
notes: Temporary terminal used from May 1852 until Michigan Central trains shifted to the Illinois Central depot at Lake Street in 1856.

address_historical: Prairie near Gurnee's tannery, opposite the Rock Island depot
notes: Built when the Michigan Southern reached Chicago in February 1852. Superseded operationally by the later joint Michigan Southern/Rock Island train shed.

address_historical: East side of Clark Street between Adams and Jackson Streets
notes: Construction began in 1850 and the frame building was completed/refitted by 1852; about 25 by 75 feet and reported cost roughly $3,000. Later moved, so demolition/fate needs parcel-level follow-up.

address_historical: Northwest corner North Avenue and Church Street
notes: Frame church approximately 40 by 60 feet, with tower and bell; reported cost $730. Enlarged around 1858 and later used as a school after a new church was built.

address_historical: Desplaines Street between Randolph and Lake Streets
notes: Dedicated July 26, 1852; about 30 by 40 feet and cost $781.33. Later sold when the congregation relocated.

address_historical: Corner Randolph and Wells Streets
notes: Built in 1853 and opened April 1854 by George H. French and John Floyd. Same hotel site was rebuilt after the fire.

address_historical: Lake Michigan at foot of Chicago Avenue
structural_system: brick engine house and brick standpipe tower
notes: Buildings and approximately 136-foot square tower were finished in 1853; water service began February 1854. Engine house about 40 by 50 feet with boiler-house wings. Model as a utility complex.

address_historical: Courthouse Square; Clark Street between Washington and Randolph Streets
owner_or_developer: Cook County and City of Chicago
notes: Cornerstone laid September 12, 1851; completed 1853. Shared city/county government complex with later cupola and public-square alterations.

address_historical: Corner Indiana Street and Wolcott Street
notes: Erected summer 1853; about 36 by 60 feet; reported $2,500 including furnishings. A school/conference building stood adjacent. Wolcott in this context was later State Street; confirm parcel.

address_historical: Northeast corner Sangamon and Owen Streets
notes: Small frame edifice about 25 by 35 feet, seating about 300, and costing roughly $800. The society formed in 1852 and had a pastor by 1853; exact completion month is not stated.

address_historical: Jackson Street at Buffalo Street
notes: Construction began September 1852; cornerstone laid April 27, 1853; dedicated November 20, 1853. Historical Buffalo Street requires street-name crosswalk before geocoding.

address_historical: Northeast corner Randolph and Dearborn Streets
notes: Opened in 1854 on the European plan; renamed Revere House in 1857. Pulled down in 1859 for the McCormick Block. Do not conflate with the later Revere at Clark and Kinzie.

address_historical: Clark Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: Double carriageway and sidewalks; cost about $12,000. Arches failed in 1855 and were repaired; bridge replaced by another Clark Street structure in 1858.

address_historical: State Street at Superior Street
notes: Cornerstone laid August 3, 1853; completed fall 1854; first Mass Christmas 1854. About 84 by 190 feet with a reported 245-foot steeple and cost near $100,000.

address_historical: Norwood Park area; outside 1854 Chicago limits
fire_fate_1871: survived; outside 1871 burn area and then-city limits
notes: Official landmark record dates the core to 1854; additions followed in 1868-75. Included in the modern-city database but it was not inside Chicago at construction.

canonical_name: Van Buren Street German Methodist Episcopal Church
address_historical: Van Buren Street at Fourth Avenue; begun at Griswold and Van Buren
notes: Construction began spring 1854 at Griswold/Van Buren; the site was sold mid-project and the building and parsonage were moved to Van Buren/Fourth Avenue and completed. Preserve both locations in future phase table.

canonical_name: First German Evangelical Lutheran Church at Polk and Edina
address_historical: Corner Polk Street and Edina Place
notes: The first congregation moved its earlier building to Clark Street in 1852, then erected this church in 1855 and worshiped here until the fire. Historical Edina Place requires street crosswalk research.

address_historical: Northwest corner Randolph and LaSalle Streets
notes: An important lecture, concert, and assembly venue. Date/location are corroborated by a historical compilation; architect and construction details remain unresolved.

address_historical: Monroe Street between Clark and South Wells (later Fifth Avenue)
architect_or_builder: Levi J. North and Harry Turner
owner_or_developer: Levi J. North and Harry Turner
notes: About 90 by 206 feet; seating 3,062; 42-foot ring; 120 gas jets; rear company rooms and horse stables. Newspaper chronology places opening on November 19, 1855.

address_historical: Twelfth Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: Rebuilt in 1855 for a reported $2,877. The source does not establish its exact removal date or 1871 condition.

address_historical: Corner Clark and Harrison Streets
notes: Built 1855-56 and opened early 1856 by J. W. Boardman; described as Chicago's only exclusively family hotel at the time. Later sold to Henry H. Honore.

address_historical: Monroe Street near Halsted Street
notes: Completed fall 1856 and opened October 8, 1856. The historical address comes from the attached chronology and should be parcel-verified; construction date and institutional use are confirmed by Andreas.

address_historical: Polk and Halsted area
fire_fate_1871: survived; west of main 1871 burn area
notes: Built as Hull's country residence in 1856; became the core of Hull-House in 1889. Official record notes later campus changes and reconstruction of missing portions, so extant authenticity is element-specific.

address_historical: 46-52 West Lake Street
notes: Built by A. Cleveland and operated with I. N. Merritt as manager; destroyed in the major 1859 fire. Do not conflate with the later Cleveland House at Clark/Kinzie.

canonical_name: German Theater at Wells and Indiana Streets
address_historical: Corner Wells and Indiana Streets
notes: Opened April 19, 1856 in a new building. The cited chronicle establishes new construction and opening but not dimensions, owner, or later fate.

address_historical: Foot of Lake Street at the lakefront
notes: Completed April 1856. Michigan Central trains also used it under agreement. Exact construction start and detailed fabric need further research.

canonical_name: Michigan Southern and Rock Island joint depot
address_historical: Van Buren Street near railroad approaches
owner_or_developer: Michigan Southern Railroad and Chicago & Rock Island Railroad
notes: Projected in October 1855 and used until October 1871. Reported 355 feet long excluding offices, 116-foot roof span, 22-foot walls, and about 42 feet to center of arch.

address_historical: Michigan Avenue at Twenty-fourth Street
fire_fate_1871: outside documented 1871 burn area; survival not established
notes: Three-story brick school erected 1856. The later school history does not state that this building burned in 1871.

address_historical: Chestnut Street north of Chicago Avenue
notes: Lot purchased and three-story brick building erected in 1856. Andreas explicitly states that the Great Fire destroyed it.

address_historical: Corner Desplaines and Adams Streets
owner_or_developer: Roman Catholic parish of St. Patrick
structural_system: stone basement; brick upper auditorium; Romanesque Revival
notes: Construction began 1854 and the church was sufficiently complete by summer 1856. Approximately 1,200 seats. Later alterations mean extant fabric should be phase-tagged.

address_historical: Jefferson Township; outside 1856 Chicago limits
fire_fate_1871: survived; outside 1871 burn area and then-city limits
notes: Official designation material dates the farmhouse circa 1856. Cupola and later changes require phase research. Included because site is now within Chicago.

address_historical: Randolph Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: A new bridge was ready for foot travel by July 1856. Additional structural and fate details were not established in this pass.

address_historical: Northwest corner South Water Street and Michigan Avenue
notes: Opened 1857; furnishing reportedly exceeded $60,000. Converted to a business block after hotel ventures failed, and remained so until October 1871.

demolition_cause: accident while driven over by cattle
address_historical: Rush Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: Contracted June 1856 for about $48,000-50,000; described as the first iron bridge in the West. Accidentally destroyed November 1863.

address_historical: Southeast corner Wells Street and Chicago Avenue
notes: The source directly states that the Second Church erected this building in 1856; dimensions, fabric, and later fate were not established in this pass.

address_historical: location not established
notes: Plain frame church about 30 by 65 feet, initially seating 300. Pews were offered September 1, 1856; the building was enlarged in 1857 to about 500 seats. Address needs parish-specific research.

address_historical: Wells Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: Completed summer 1856; about 190 feet and reported cost $20,000; described as the longest drawbridge in the West. Replacement/removal date needs bridge-specific study.

address_historical: Michigan Avenue; exact corner not established
notes: Built in 1857 and opened autumn 1858 by William Adams. Andreas confirms destruction but the excerpt used here does not supply a precise street number/corner.

address_historical: Morgan Park area; outside 1857 Chicago limits
fire_fate_1871: survived; outside 1871 burn area and then-city limits
notes: Official landmark record dates the house to 1857; front bay and rear wing were added in the 1870s. Included because site is now within Chicago.

address_historical: 241-243 South Desplaines Street between Van Buren and Harrison Streets
notes: Dedicated July 26, 1857; about 45 by 70 feet with a large steeple, cost roughly $5,200. Sold to a Lutheran congregation after the Methodist society moved.

address_historical: Erie Street crossing
notes: Built during the 1856-57 bridge program; reported cost about $5,000. Exact completion date and removal history unresolved.

canonical_name: First German Methodist Episcopal Church on Clybourn Avenue
address_historical: Clybourn Avenue; exact parcel not established
notes: Wood building about 30 by 50 feet and cost roughly $2,000. Moved to the back of the lot in 1863 when a brick church replaced it; Andreas states the fire swept away all church property.

address_historical: Union Street near Twelfth Street
fire_fate_1871: outside documented 1871 burn area; survival not established
notes: Three-story brick building erected in 1857 for $28,000, replacing/supplementing a two-story wooden 1855 schoolhouse. Named Foster School in 1858. The attached timeline's 1856 date is not supported by Andreas.

address_historical: Indiana Street crossing
notes: Built during the 1856-57 bridge program; reported cost about $5,000. Historical street and crossing require geospatial reconciliation.

address_historical: Madison Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: Built 1857; reported 155 feet and cost $42,000. Bridge-specific replacement chronology remains to be established.

address_historical: Southwest corner Central Avenue and South Water Street
owner_or_developer: David A. Gage and George W. Gage
structural_system: brick, exterior plastered and tiled to imitate stone
notes: Opened in 1858 by John C. Parks and John W. Humphreys; 72 rooms and reported cost $32,000. OCR says a 1851 sale, an obvious typographical error inconsistent with the 1857 construction; not propagated.

address_historical: Madison Street between State and Dearborn Streets
notes: Opened November 5, 1857; reported cost $85,000, seating about 2,500, and stage about 80 by 53 feet. Substantially altered in 1864 before its 1871 destruction.

address_historical: Polk Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: Built during the 1856-57 bridge program; reported cost about $5,000. Exact completion date unresolved.

address_historical: Southeast corner Cass and Huron Streets
notes: Completed and opened December 1857; reported cost $60,000 excluding land and tower. Cass Street later became Wabash Avenue in this area; confirm address crosswalk.

address_historical: Clark Street crossing of the Chicago River
notes: Constructed in 1858 to replace the troubled 1854 pivot bridge. Further structural and removal chronology needs bridge-specific research.

address_historical: Southeast corner Wabash Avenue and Madison Street
notes: First kept as a hotel in 1858 by Joshua Barrell; construction may slightly predate hotel use, so 1858 is not asserted as an exact build date. Enlarged after 1861.

address_historical: Chicago City Cemetery
address_modern: Lincoln Park, south of N. LaSalle Drive on axis with N. Stockton Drive
architect_or_builder: John M. Van Osdel and Frederick Baumann
fire_fate_1871: survived; within later North Side fire area but mausoleum remained
notes: Official Park District record identifies installation in 1858 and a roughly fifty-ton structure. It is the principal above-ground remnant of the former City Cemetery; restored in 1999.

address_historical: Corner Orchard and Willow Streets
fire_fate_1871: survived at edge of Great Fire; used as hospital and relief depot
notes: Erected 1858 and opened January 1859. Andreas says it stood on the northwest border of the fire limits and sheltered fire victims; it therefore survived the conflagration. Later demolition date not established here.

address_historical: Northwest corner Wabash Avenue and Harrison Street
notes: Cornerstone laid July 13, 1857; completed and dedicated July 15, 1858. Successor to the State Street Methodist congregation; $32,555 was initially subscribed for construction.

canonical_name: Old University of Chicago south wing
address_historical: West side Cottage Grove Avenue just north of 35th Street
fire_fate_1871: survived; south of Great Chicago Fire burn area
notes: Cornerstone of the university building laid July 4, 1857; the south wing was completed for classes in 1859. Critical correction: the main Douglas Hall and observatory were not complete until 1864, so this record covers only the first wing.

address_historical: 281-285 State Street
notes: First appears as a hotel in the 1859 city directory, operated by L. L. Atwood. This does not prove the building itself was newly constructed in 1859; retain as an occupancy record pending permit/deed research.

address_historical: 22-24 North Wells Street
